template.name: Linear Programming Duality: Construction Rules and Duality Theorems
template.description: For a primal–dual pair in linear programming, construct the dual by transposing the constraint matrix, interchanging the objective coefficients and the right-hand sides of the constraints, and reversing the optimization direction: a minimization primal corresponds to a maximization dual. The dual of the dual returns to the primal. Weak duality states the ordering relation between the objective value of every dual-feasible solution and the optimal value, while strong duality states that the two problems have equal optimal values when the relevant optimal solutions exist. In multiple-choice questions, each statement about the dual construction must be checked separately and precisely.
applicability: A problem asks for the dual of a linear program or for a judgment about primal–dual conversion.
The question concerns the transpose of the constraint matrix, the destination of the right-hand side, objective coefficients, or the optimization direction.
Weak duality or strong duality is needed to compare feasible objective values or optimal values.

steps.step: Identify the primal matrix, coefficients, and optimization direction
steps.detail: Record the constraint matrix, the objective-function coefficient vector, the right-hand-side vector, the inequality directions, and whether the primal is a minimization or maximization problem.

steps.step: Construct the dual component by component
steps.detail: Transpose the constraint matrix; exchange the roles of the primal objective coefficients and constraint right-hand sides; and reverse the optimization direction, so a minimization primal has a maximization dual.
Verify that applying the construction a second time returns the original primal problem, including its matrix orientation, coefficients, directions, and optimization type.

steps.step: Apply weak and strong duality precisely
steps.detail: Use weak duality for the inequality between the objective value of a dual-feasible solution and the appropriate optimum, and use strong duality only for equality of the two optimal values under its conditions.

steps.step: Audit verbal statements one by one
steps.detail: Do not accept an imprecise claim such as ‘the objective function becomes a constraint.’ The primal objective coefficients become the right-hand sides of dual constraints; the primal constraint right-hand sides enter the dual objective; and the constraint matrix itself is transposed.

template.name: Translation-Invariant Total Orders and Parity Analysis of Rank Functions
template.description: A bijection with translation-order-preserving behavior is equivalent to a translation-invariant total order. Such an order is determined by a positive cone and can be represented as layers of a linear functional together with a tie-breaking rule inside every layer. Its rank function decomposes into a layer count plus an in-layer offset. This decomposition permits exact parity counting of ranks on a target rectangular region. One must range over the feasible parameter family consisting of coprime slopes and tie-breaking rules and optimize over that family. The count N varies with the coprime parameters (p,q) and the tie-breaking direction between N_min and N_max; the two extremes are attained by the two tie-breaking choices for an extreme slope of type (1,q). If the requested quantity is a product or combination of endpoint values, both endpoints must be found by traversing the parameter family rather than evaluating only one parameter choice.
applicability: A problem concerns an order-preserving bijection that is invariant under translations, or an equivalent translation-invariant total order.
The order is described by a coprime linear-functional slope (p,q) and an in-layer tie-breaking rule such as smaller x first versus smaller y first.
The task counts even or odd rank values on a rectangular target region, especially one with half-open interval boundaries.
The required result depends on extrema over all admissible order parameters.

steps.step: Replace the order-preserving bijection by a translation-invariant total order
steps.detail: Use the equivalence in the correct direction: the translation-order-preserving bijection induces a translation-invariant total order, and conversely the order determines the corresponding ranking behavior.

steps.step: Parameterize the order by layers and a tie-break
steps.detail: Choose a linear functional with coprime slope parameters (p,q), use its values as layer indices, and specify the in-layer rule, for example whether smaller x or smaller y is placed first.
Write each rank as the number of points in earlier layers plus the offset within the current layer. Keep these two terms separate when computing parity.

steps.step: Count parity by layer index and offset
steps.detail: For every point in the target rectangle, classify the parity of the layer contribution and the in-layer offset, then combine the two parities. Respect half-open boundary conventions exactly.

Compute the count for each admissible coprime slope and each tie-breaking direction. The values range from N_min to N_max, with endpoint values attained by the two tie-breaks for an extreme slope of type (1,q); do not infer the answer from a single parameter setting.

template.name: Digit DP for Divisibility Counting with Restricted Digit Sets
template.description: To count natural numbers whose number of digits is at most a specified bound, whose digits belong to a finite digit set, and whose value satisfies divisibility by a small modulus, use digit-by-digit dynamic programming. The state is the remainder modulo the modulus of the processed digit sum or numerical value, and transitions are performed one digit at a time. Transition coefficients are determined by the residues modulo the modulus contributed by digits in the allowed set. The key distinction is between counting strings that allow leading zeroes and counting genuine natural numbers: the leading digit cannot be zero. The correction is: the number of valid natural numbers of length L equals the number of valid strings of length L minus the number of valid strings of length L−1. Finally, treat whether 0 itself is included according to the problem statement.
applicability: The three features ‘restricted digit set + divisibility by a small integer + bounded digit length’ occur together.
The modulus is small, often a one-digit integer, so remainder can be used directly as a DP-state dimension.
Several allowed digits can have the same residue modulo the modulus, allowing transitions to be compressed by residue frequency.

steps.detail: When the digit set is finite, the number must be divisible by a small modulus, and the number of digits has an upper bound, use a position-by-position DP rather than direct enumeration of strings.
Track the remainder modulo the modulus of the processed digit sum or processed numerical value, using the update rule appropriate to the divisibility condition.

For every allowed digit, compute its residue modulo the modulus. If multiple digits have the same residue, count the number of occurrences of each residue first and use those counts as transition coefficients.

steps.step: Count strings with leading zeroes first
steps.detail: Run the DP for length L while allowing zero in every position to obtain the count of valid digit strings of length L.

Because the first digit of a natural number cannot be zero, use valid_natural_numbers(L) = valid_strings(L) − valid_strings(L−1). Sum the required lengths from 1 to the specified upper bound with correct endpoints.

Check separately whether 0 is included by the problem statement. Avoid direct string enumeration without remainder classes, omitted leading-zero correction, and off-by-one errors in the length summation.

template.name: Classification of Integer-Valued Functions Under Divisibility Constraints
template.description: If an integer-valued function g satisfies the condition that, for every pair of distinct integers a,b, the difference g(a)−g(b) divides the corresponding difference of powers, then all solutions have power-function-family form: g is x raised to the d-th power, where d ranges over the divisors of the specified positive integer, or a mirror/translation variant of such a power function. When the exponent and power satisfy particular parity conditions, there is an additional signed family. The number of functions is twice the number of divisors when the exponent contains no factor 2. When it contains a power-of-2 factor, writing the exponent as its 2-adic part times its odd part gives twice the product of twice the 2-adic exponent and the number of divisors of the odd part. The condition that this number is 2 times an odd integer is equivalent to the divisor count being odd, hence to the positive integer being a perfect square. Combined with the parity constraint, this frequently reduces to odd perfect squares.
applicability: An integer-valued function is constrained by divisibility of differences g(a)−g(b) by differences of powers for all distinct integers a,b.
The task requires classification of all functions, counting the families, or locating the N-th positive integer with a stated count property.
The exponent has parity or 2-adic structure relevant to the number of solution families.

steps.detail: Start from the power functions g(x)=x^d for every divisor d of the specified positive integer, together with their mirror/translation variants.
Analyze the specified parity relation between exponent and power. Include the additional signed solution family when that parity condition holds; do not omit it.
If the exponent has no factor 2, the total is 2 times the divisor count. If it has a 2-adic factor and an odd part, use 2 times twice the 2-adic exponent times the divisor count of the odd part.

steps.step: Convert the requested count property into a divisor property
steps.detail: Use count = 2 × odd if and only if the divisor count is odd, which holds if and only if the integer is a perfect square. Combine this with any parity restriction.

steps.step: Invert an ordinal only after deriving the sequence
steps.detail: For the resulting odd-perfect-square sequence, the N-th term is (2N−1)^2. Check N=1,2,3, obtaining 1,9,25, before substituting the requested ordinal; do not use N^2 directly.

template.name: Prime Divisibility in Recurrences and Coprime Linear-Combination Norms
template.description: Two recurring lines of argument are useful. (a) For coprime integers k,l, the coefficient-norm function defined by min |a|+|b| subject to ka+lb=x measures the shortest representation of an integer with respect to the generating pair. The number of ‘nice’ integers satisfying a local-maximum condition depends only on the smaller parameter and on the parity case: both parameters odd versus one parameter even. The corresponding counting formulas differ by a multiplicative factor arising from symmetry. (b) To prove that every prime divides some term of a linear recurrence, first derive its closed form as a homogeneous solution plus a particular solution, reducing it to a power sum plus a constant. Then use Fermat's little theorem and modular periodicity to find, for every prime, an exponent index at which that prime divides the designated term. In the norm-equation ending, reduce to (αy−βd)^2+γt^2=δd^2; solution parity is determined by a divisibility condition of type 14|d, and typical counts simplify as F=l−1 and G=2(l−1), giving a target expression of type p^2+q^2=5(l−1)^2 for l.
applicability: Coprime coefficients k,l define representations ka+lb=x and the objective is min |a|+|b| or a local-extremum count.
A recurrence must be shown to have a term divisible by every prime.
A statement about integers coprime to all terms needs reduction to prime factors and separate modular arguments.
The final calculation reduces to a quadratic or imaginary-quadratic norm equation with parity and divisibility conditions.

steps.step: Treat the coefficient norm as the primary object
steps.detail: For ka+lb=x with gcd(k,l)=1, study min |a|+|b| as a function of x rather than attempting only isolated Diophantine solutions.
Derive the count for the cases ‘both k and l odd’ and ‘one even’ separately. The ratio between the formulas follows from symmetry; combining the cases prematurely gives an incorrect proportion.

steps.step: Derive the recurrence closed form exactly
steps.detail: Solve the recurrence as homogeneous solution plus particular solution, retaining the constant term and all coefficients, and rewrite it as a power sum plus a constant.

For each prime, use Fermat's little theorem and modular periodicity to select an exponent index for which the designated recurrence term is divisible by that prime. Do not extrapolate from checks of a few small primes, and do not confuse ‘every prime divides some term’ with ‘one prime divides every term.’

Reduce the coefficient-norm relation to (αy−βd)^2+γt^2=δd^2. Use a condition of type 14|d to decide solution parity, then apply F=l−1 and G=2(l−1) when those counts arise, yielding the target form p^2+q^2=5(l−1)^2.

template.name: Floor Inequalities via Complete Residue Systems
template.description: For inequalities required to hold in every residue class, change the traversal index so that it runs from 1 to p−1 and use the complete-residue-system property modulo a prime p: after setting j=k+1, the residues of n·j modulo p still run through all nonzero residue classes. Rewrite the inequality as a condition that, for every j, the residue is at least a linear threshold. Via residue = original quantity − modulus × floor, this is equivalent to a uniform upper bound on a floor quotient. All admissible n form the decreasing sequence of floor values ⌊p/j⌋ for consecutive integers j. Therefore the k-th largest admissible value is ⌊p/k⌋. This conclusion requires explicit verification for k=1,2 and correct treatment of repeated values in the floor sequence.
applicability: An inequality is required for every residue class modulo a prime p.
Replacing k by j=k+1 converts the relevant terms into a complete nonzero residue system.
The problem asks for an upper bound on floor quotients or for the k-th largest admissible integer.

steps.detail: Set j=k+1 so the index traverses 1 through p−1. When n<p, multiplication by n permutes the nonzero residues modulo the prime p; this prerequisite must be checked.
Let r=nj mod p. Use r = nj − p⌊nj/p⌋ to convert the lower bound on r into the required uniform upper bound for a floor expression. Preserve the inequality direction.
The admissible n are exactly the decreasing values of the form ⌊p/j⌋ as j=1,2,3,… increases.
The k-th largest value is ⌊p/k⌋. Check k=1 and k=2 by writing the two largest admissible values before applying the general formula; ⌊p/(k+1)⌋ is the common one-position error.
The sequence ⌊p/j⌋ can contain repeated values, so count ranks using the ordered sequence and its multiplicities rather than treating all quotient values as distinct.

template.name: Digit Structure in Long Division with Zero-Free Dividends
template.description: For division with remainder in which the dividend has a fixed number of decimal digits and no zero digit, analyze the decimal structure of the quotient. If the quotient has L digits and t nonzero digits, and the divisor has d digits, view multiplication as the position-shifted superposition of one copy of the divisor for every nonzero quotient digit. These copies must cover every digit position of the dividend without producing a zero digit, yielding a coverage inequality relating t·d and L. Maximizing the number A=L−t of zero digits in the quotient becomes a discrete optimization that balances L and t under the digit budget. If L is too large, each copy covers too little; if L is too small, digits are wasted. At the optimum, nonzero quotient digits are approximately equally spaced. One must still verify whether carries fill the gaps and how the remainder corrects the last digit. The closing bound is t·d≥L, followed by a construction with nonuniform gaps and carry filling, and a proof that if A+1 gaps are too large they cannot be filled (the 939-type ending).
applicability: A fixed-length dividend with no zero digit is divided with remainder, and the task asks about zero versus nonzero digits of the quotient.
The divisor digit length d, quotient length L, and number t of nonzero quotient digits can be related by shifted multiplication copies.
A sharp upper bound and a construction attaining it are both required.

steps.detail: Expand quotient times divisor as one d-digit divisor copy for each nonzero quotient digit, shifted according to that digit's position.
Because the copies must cover the full dividend without creating zero positions, obtain t·d≥L. Treat this as an inequality, not an equality.
Set A=L−t and optimize over feasible integer values of L and t. Balance the loss from overly large L against wasted digit budget from overly small L.
Use approximately equal spacing, allowing nonuniform gaps where necessary, and verify that carries can fill the intervening positions and that the remainder corrects the final digit.

steps.step: Prove optimality in the opposite direction
steps.detail: After the construction reaches the candidate bound, prove that A+1 gaps would be too large to fill, using the 939-type terminal argument. Do not give a construction without an upper-bound proof.

template.name: Line Covers of Planar Point Sets and an Erdős–de Bruijn-Type Bound
template.description: Consider a planar point set S which cannot be covered altogether by a specified number of lines, has no circle through all its points, but becomes coverable by the same number of lines after deletion of any one point. To maximize |S|, take a family of lines in general position—no two parallel and no three concurrent—and let S be the set of all pairwise intersections. After one intersection is deleted, every remaining intersection lies on the lines other than the two that determined the deleted point, so the deletion-cover condition holds automatically. The absence of a circle through all points is an additional condition that must be verified separately. An Erdős–de Bruijn-type theorem gives a quadratic-in-the-number-of-lines upper bound for such covering conditions, and the number of pairwise intersections in the construction attains that bound.
applicability: A point set is globally not coverable by a prescribed number of lines, while deletion of any one point makes it coverable by that same number.
The problem includes an additional nonconcyclicity condition.
A maximum cardinality is sought under line-cover incidence constraints.

steps.detail: The symmetric condition ‘not coverable as a whole, but coverable after deletion of any point’ suggests taking all pairwise intersections of a line family.
Require no parallel lines and no three lines through one point. Otherwise both the intersection count and the deletion-cover structure change.
When an intersection determined by two lines is removed, retain all the other lines; every other pairwise intersection lies on at least one retained line.
Explicitly rule out a circle passing through all chosen intersections; it is not implied by the covering argument.

steps.step: Match construction with the upper bound
steps.detail: Use point–line incidence counting or an Erdős–de Bruijn-type theorem to obtain the quadratic upper bound in the number of lines. When it equals the pairwise-intersection count, the construction is extremal.

template.name: Angle Subdivision and Segment Ratios in a Right Triangle
template.description: In a right triangle, choose two points on one leg so that the endpoint of the hypotenuse subtends prescribed split angles at those points, and determine the ratio of the two intercepted segments. Decompose the diagram according to the positions of the two subtended angles into two small triangles. In each triangle, use the sine rule to express the target segment as the adjacent leg or hypotenuse divided by the sine of its corresponding angle. Then use right-triangle relations—complementary acute angles and the interchange of sine and cosine—to express both segments in terms of one reference length. Finally simplify the sine ratio with a double-angle identity. The resulting ratio is independent of the size of the original triangle and is a constant.
applicability: A right triangle contains two points on a leg, with given angle subdivision at the hypotenuse endpoint.
The task asks for a ratio of segments cut off by rays rather than an absolute length.
The prescribed angles permit sine-rule evaluation and double-angle simplification.

steps.step: Draw and order the subtended rays correctly
steps.detail: The order of the two points determines the geometric angle configuration. Mark the two rays from the hypotenuse endpoint before assigning angles.

steps.step: Apply the sine rule in each small triangle
steps.detail: For each target segment, pair every side with its opposite angle exactly; express it through the relevant adjacent leg or hypotenuse and a sine ratio.

steps.step: Move to a common reference length
steps.detail: Use complementary acute angles in the right triangle to interchange sine and cosine as needed, so both segment expressions use the same base length.
Cancel the common length and use the required double-angle formula, retaining all coefficients.
Verify the requested numerator and denominator against the statement. A reversed point order, mismatched opposite angle, or omitted double-angle coefficient invalidates the result.

template.name: Distribution of Vertex Area-Bisectors in a Convex Polygon
template.description: In a convex polygon, draw from every vertex the segment that bisects the polygonal area and meets the opposite boundary. The distribution of the resulting endpoints is controlled by a continuity-and-partition argument: as the area-bisector continuously sweeps the polygon, the boundary edges receiving endpoints from the vertices form at most a constant number of consecutive blocks in boundary order. Consequently all endpoints lie on at most three edges, independently of the number n of polygon sides. The minimum is therefore the constant 3: for n=3 this is the median case, and for n≥4 a nearly degenerate construction attains exactly three receiving edges. The area bisector need not pass through the midpoint of the opposite side.
applicability: A convex n-gon has one area-bisecting segment from each vertex to the opposite boundary.
The problem asks for the smallest possible number of boundary edges containing all intersection endpoints.
Continuity and boundary-order arguments can show that the quantity is independent of n.

steps.step: Distinguish an area bisector from a median
steps.detail: The segment halves polygonal area but is not required to pass through the midpoint of its opposite boundary side.

steps.step: Use continuous sweeping along the boundary
steps.detail: Track the endpoint of the vertex area-bisector as the relevant vertex position varies. Use continuity to organize receiving edges into consecutive boundary segments.

steps.step: Count receiving-edge blocks in boundary order
steps.detail: The continuity partition bounds all endpoints by three edges. Include cases in which an endpoint coincides with a polygon vertex so no edge is over- or under-counted.
For n=3 use the median configuration. For every n≥4 give a nearly degenerate convex construction in which endpoints occur on exactly three edges.
The minimum is 3 for all n; it is a constant, not a function of n.

template.name: Compatibility of Congruent Triangle Dissections and Tangential Polygons
template.description: When a convex polygon is dissected by nonintersecting diagonals into congruent triangles, the dissection structure—the number of triangles and the number of triangle angles meeting at every vertex—is determined by the number of sides. Congruence forces every polygonal interior angle to be an integer-multiple allocation of one common set of triangle angles. If the polygon must also be tangential to a circle, hence possess an incircle, it must satisfy the equality of sums of opposite sides or concurrence of angle bisectors. The two requirements are compatible only in the smallest side-number case: the symmetry forced by the congruent dissection gives a kite, and imposing the tangency condition forces all four sides equal, producing a special quadrilateral that always has an incircle. For larger numbers of sides, exclude possibilities case by case using total angle measure or broken symmetry.
applicability: A convex polygon is triangulated by pairwise nonintersecting diagonals into congruent triangles.
The polygon is additionally required to be tangential, meaning that it has an incircle rather than merely a circumcircle.
The goal is to determine all feasible numbers of sides.

steps.detail: Use the number of congruent triangles and the number of triangle angles incident at each polygon vertex to express each interior angle as an integer-multiple allocation.
For a tangential polygon use equality of opposite-side sums or concurrence of angle bisectors. Do not confuse this with cyclicity, which concerns a circumcircle.
In the smallest side-number case, the congruent dissection enforces kite symmetry; after imposing tangency, all four sides are forced equal, giving the special quadrilateral with an incircle.
For each larger number of sides, use the total angle sum or the failure of the required symmetry to rule out compatibility.
Congruent triangles can contribute different numbers of angles at different polygon vertices, so verify each interior-angle sum rather than assuming uniform incidence.

template.name: Angle-Multiple Relations and Solution Counts in a Collinear Configuration
template.description: Choose a moving point on the line containing a segment so that two subtended angles satisfy a multiple relation, with one angle exactly half the other. Geometrically this is a ray-trisection picture. Convert every ratio relation by the sine rule or similarity into an equation for the position of the moving point, measured as a distance from the intersection. Once the inclination of the fixed line is fixed, every relation has at most one solution on each ray, that is, on each of the two directions from the point. There are two possible angle relations and two ray directions, giving an upper bound of 4. All four solutions occur when the endpoint-distance ratio lies in a compatibility interval of type (1/2,2) and the line inclination is suitable; outside that interval the number can drop abruptly.
applicability: A moving point lies on the line of a segment, and two subtended angles have a 2-to-1 relation.
The task asks for the number or maximum number of geometric solutions.
Endpoint distances from an intersection and the inclination of a fixed line determine compatibility.

steps.detail: ‘The larger angle is twice the smaller’ and its reversed placement are different cases and must both be considered.

steps.step: Split the line into two rays
steps.detail: A moving point can occur in either direction from the intersection. For each fixed relation, prove there is at most one solution per ray.
Use the sine rule or similar triangles to rewrite the angle-ratio condition as an equation in the distance from the intersection.
Determine when solutions from all relations and both directions coexist. The endpoint-distance ratio must lie in an interval of type (1/2,2), and the inclination must be appropriate.
Two relations times two directions gives at most 4 solutions. Give a compatible configuration attaining 4 rather than merely counting the upper bound.

template.name: Face Visibility of Convex Polyhedra via Normal-Vector Separation
template.description: From an exterior observation point, a face of a convex polyhedron is visible exactly when its outward normal has positive dot product with the viewing direction. Requiring that every face have an observation point from which all other faces are visible while that face alone is hidden is equivalent to requiring that each face normal be separable from all other normals by a hyperplane through the origin. In three dimensions this property is possible only for a simplex normal configuration, dual to a tetrahedron. Hence the minimum possible number of faces is 4. For a tetrahedron, verify the construction face by face by choosing, for every face, an observation point close to that face and outside the other three faces. The point must lie strictly in the exterior half-space of the hidden face.
applicability: A convex polyhedron is viewed from exterior points and a visibility condition isolates one hidden face at a time.
The problem asks for a minimum number of faces under visibility constraints.
Face visibility can be converted to dot products of outward normals and linear separation.

steps.detail: A face is visible when its outward normal has positive dot product with the viewing direction. Encode the condition for every face separately.

Use convex-cone or separation results, such as Carathéodory-type reasoning, to show that a three-dimensional configuration with this property is a simplex normal configuration.

template.name: Common Points of Three Circles and Parametric Tangent Circles
template.description: For a parameterized family of circles, three circles have exactly two common points precisely when each pair meets in the same pair of points, equivalently when the circles are coaxal. Test this through coincident common chords or concurrent radical axes. If one circle passes through a fixed point and is tangent to a fixed circle at a prescribed tangency point, its center lies on the normal through that tangency point, and its radius is uniquely determined by the fixed point. Thus the center and radius of the family are explicit functions of the parameter. Write the coaxality condition algebraically and solve for every parameter value. In the unit-circumcircle coordinate setup, scan the coaxality discriminant over values such as k∈[0.1,3] to locate candidates k=1/2 and k=1, then supply the geometric proof through midpoint and excenter configurations. The answer commonly consists of two fractional values, both of which must be reported.
applicability: A family of circles is constrained by a fixed point and tangency to a fixed circle at a specified point.

Place the center on the normal line through the fixed tangency point; use the condition of passing through the fixed point to determine the radius explicitly.

template.name: Tangents, Arc Midpoints, and Angle Closure on the Circumcircle of a Right Triangle
template.description: The circumcircle of a right triangle has the hypotenuse as a diameter by Thales' theorem. In the configuration chain ‘a tangent at a vertex meets the extension of the opposite side; take the midpoint of the minor arc; join it and meet the circle again; a tangent at the new intersection meets the other leg; determine an angle,’ repeatedly use three tools: an arc midpoint is equidistant from arc endpoints and gives the corresponding angle-bisector relation; the tangent–chord angle theorem; and the fact that an angle subtended by a diameter is a right angle. The angle chain often closes to a right angle independently of the triangle's shape. A coordinate method placing the circumcenter at the origin and the hypotenuse on an axis converts the chain into line–circle intersections, with angles read from slopes or vector dot products.
applicability: A right triangle has a construction involving its circumcircle, tangents, a minor-arc midpoint, and a second circle intersection.
The task asks for an angle, and hidden right angles or isosceles relations are likely.
A synthetic tangent–chord proof or a coordinate line–circle computation is available.

steps.detail: Mark the hypotenuse as a diameter of the circumcircle and immediately record the resulting right inscribed angles.
Use the midpoint of the minor arc, not the major arc. The two choices give supplementary branches, and the arc midpoint is equidistant from its endpoints.

steps.step: Apply tangent–chord angles with the matching chord

steps.step: Use coordinates as a verification route
steps.detail: Put the circumcenter at the origin and the hypotenuse on a coordinate axis, solve the line–circle intersections, then read the target angle from slopes or a vector dot product.

template.name: Polar Envelopes for the Orthocenter Circle Configuration
template.description: Let three circles be centered at the vertices of a triangle, with radii equal to the respective distances from those vertices to the orthocenter. The key degeneration is that a polar line becomes the tangent at the point whenever the point lies on its circle. The orthocenter M lies on all three circles because each radius was defined as the distance to M. Thus at the special position Y=M, the three polar lines are the three tangents; they form a triangle whose circumcircle passes through M. This establishes M as a locus point. A numerical scan finds no other points, so the locus is the singleton {M}, not a curve. template.name: Convex Quadrilateral Area via Diagonals and Perimeter-Constrained Optimization
template.description: The area of a convex quadrilateral can be decomposed into the areas of two triangles along a diagonal, and can also be written as S=½·d₁d₂·sinθ, where d₁,d₂ are the diagonal lengths and θ is their included angle. template.name: Latin Squares with Inter-Row Difference Constraints
template.description: Fill a table row by row with permutations of n symbols, requiring each row to be a permutation and each column to have distinct entries; this is a Latin square. Column distinctness immediately bounds the number of rows by n. A condition that any two rows have a difference at least a prescribed threshold in at least one column excludes pairs of adjacent permutations, namely pairs whose entrywise differences are all too small to meet the threshold. When the row count reaches its maximum, the table is an n×n Latin square, and the required enumeration is the number of Latin squares satisfying the difference condition. Fixing the first row removes the full-row permutation symmetry before counting. The condition means ‘at least one column meets the threshold,’ not ‘every column meets it.’

template.description: For a real tuple, rewrite the sum of pairwise products through the identity Σ_{p<q} c_p c_q=[(Σc)^2−Σc^2]/2. template.name: Special-Value Substitution and Polynomialization of Functional Equations
template.description: For a two-variable functional equation, first substitute special values that eliminate one variable, such as zero or a unit, to obtain one-variable constraints. This either rules out constant candidates or fixes critical initial values. Then substitute paired values such as opposites and subtract the resulting equations to eliminate terms at antipodal points, yielding a recurrence. Use it to prove that every solution is a polynomial with bounded degree. Finally write a general polynomial, compare coefficients to get a finite candidate list, and substitute every candidate back into the original equation. Both necessity—no other solutions—and sufficiency—each candidate works—must be established.
applicability: A functional equation has two variables and special substitutions can remove one of them.
Opposite or paired arguments permit subtraction that eliminates symmetric terms.
The objective is to classify all solutions, often by proving they are polynomials of controlled degree.

steps.step: Eliminate variables in the right order
steps.detail: First choose zero, one, or another special input that removes a variable; then determine initial values or rule out constant branches before using paired substitutions.

Use arguments that are negatives of one another or otherwise paired to cancel antipodal terms and derive a recurrence.

template.name: Edge-Flip Propagation on Rational Graphs and Continued-Fraction Reduction
template.description: Let a function on the rational numbers take values in a binary field and require unequal values at the two ends of each of three edge types: negation, complement, and reciprocal. The value at one point determines the entire function uniquely by connectivity of the graph; edge flips are exactly a graph two-coloring. To evaluate the function at an arbitrary rational, reduce it by a continued-fraction/Euclidean procedure: repeatedly subtract the integer part, which does not change the function value, and take the reciprocal, which flips the value, until reaching a constant. The parity of the number of reciprocal operations determines whether the value agrees with the initial value or is flipped. Finally sum values in the binary field, using parity arithmetic rather than decimal carrying.
applicability: A rational-valued graph has negation, complement, and reciprocal edges, and a binary-valued function flips across every such edge.
The task asks for values at rationals or their binary-field sum.
Continued fractions or Euclidean reduction can reduce each rational to a base point.

steps.step: Model constraints as a graph two-coloring
steps.detail: Each required unequal edge flips the binary value. Use graph connectivity to prove uniqueness from one initial value.
Subtracting the integer part leaves the function value unchanged; perform this operation before counting reciprocal steps.
Every reciprocal operation flips the value. The parity of their number determines the relation to the base value.
Repeat the unchanged subtraction and flip-producing reciprocal steps until a constant rational is reached.
Combine values with binary-field parity rules, not ordinary decimal carries. Do not confuse unchanged integer-part subtraction with the reciprocal flip.

template.name: Logarithmic Differentiation and Partial Fractions for Excluding Real Roots
template.description: For a real-coefficient polynomial F, use logarithmic differentiation to expand F′/F as the partial-fraction sum of reciprocals of the roots. Differentiating again gives (F′/F)′=(F″F−F′²)/F² and hence F″F−F′²=−F²·Σ1/(z−α)^2. For real z away from the roots this is strictly negative, as the expression is the negative of a sum of squares times F². At a simple root, F=0 but F′≠0, so the sign can also be determined directly. Thus equations containing products of F and its first and second derivatives can be shown to have no real solutions without knowing the individual roots. Root points and nonroot intervals must be handled separately.
applicability: A real polynomial equation contains F, F′, and F″ in a product combination such as F″F−F′².
The goal is to determine whether the equation has real roots without explicitly solving for the roots of F.
Partial fractions of the logarithmic derivative are available.

steps.detail: Write F′/F as the sum of reciprocal terms 1/(z−α) over the roots, with the correct sign convention.
Use (F′/F)′=(F″F−F′²)/F² to obtain F″F−F′²=−F²·Σ1/(z−α)^2.

template.name: Polynomial Invariants Under Parameter Transformations
template.description: When a bivariate polynomial f is required to take equal values on two classes of parameter points, first translate the correspondence between points into a coordinate transformation. If that transformation preserves two basic symmetric invariants—a sum-type invariant and an invariant constructed from a product and a squared difference—then two parameter points lie in the same orbit if and only if both invariants agree. The full solution set is exactly the ring of polynomials expressible in these two invariants. Prove both directions: every solution satisfying the original condition must be a polynomial in the invariant generators, and every polynomial in those generators satisfies the condition.

The transformation preserves a sum-type invariant and a product/difference-square-type invariant.

template.name: Power Reduction and Minimal Polynomials in a Cubic Radical Extension
template.description: For a number x that is the sum of two cubic radicals, choose a basis of the extension and reduce every cube of an individual radical to a constant. Repeated power reduction expresses every power of x as a linear combination of basis elements, yielding an integer-coefficient polynomial equation for x and hence its minimal polynomial. To find a polynomial for a target quantity such as x divided by one radical, first express that quantity in basis coordinates. Then take an undetermined polynomial of the lowest feasible degree, expand its value in the same basis, and compare coordinates. Linear independence of the basis gives a linear system for the coefficients; solve it and substitute back to verify. One must compute the multiplication table correctly, retain cross terms in powers of x, continually reduce higher powers into the basis, and prove that the degree cannot be lowered further.

A basis of a cubic-radical field extension can be chosen, with cube powers reduced to constants.

template.name: Solution Orbits and Counting for Symmetric Polynomial Systems
template.description: For a cyclically symmetric multivariable polynomial system, first exploit the fact that cyclic permutations and simultaneous sign reversal preserve the solution set. Elimination may introduce components not belonging to the original system, so every counted root must be checked back in the system.

template.name: Closure Generated by Vector Addition and Coordinatewise Maximum
template.description: For integer vectors with both addition and coordinatewise maximum allowed, the set generated by initial vectors has a lattice-plus-semilattice structure. One or two initial vectors generate only a low-rank sublattice and cannot cover the full integer-vector space. Three vectors suffice: a constant vector with all coordinates equal, an alternating-sign vector, and a strictly increasing vector. By alternating addition and coordinatewise maximum, construct every standard basis vector coordinate by coordinate, then obtain every integer vector by linear combination.
